name: Formats, Examples, and Avatars
title: Formats, Examples, and Avatars
answer: This idea covers three ways to make personalized lessons more accessible and meaningful: offering content in multiple formats, using AI to suggest examples connected to students' lives, and choosing tutor avatars carefully. It matters because access should not depend on a supposed learning style, examples must be accurate and respectful, and avatar features can shape trust for reasons unrelated to help quality. Schools can use AI to generate options while teachers keep the judgment about accuracy, respect, and student connection.

sections.body: The idea is that personalization can be supported by presenting the same lesson in more than one format, such as text, audio through Microsoft Immersive Reader, and a visual summary. It also involves asking AI for examples tied to the community, class interests, or students' cultures so that learning feels more meaningful. A third part concerns tutor avatars, because the race, gender, and age of an AI tutor's avatar can affect how much learners trust it and whether they follow its guidance. The problem it solves is access and relevance without pretending that students have fixed learning styles that teaching must match. It also helps schools avoid building irrelevant biases into tutoring before students ever judge the quality of the help.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher can offer the same lesson as text, as audio through Microsoft Immersive Reader, and as a visual summary so more students can reach the material. The teacher can ask AI for examples connected to the local community, the interests of the class, or the cultures students come from, then check each example for accuracy and respect. The text does not give grade bands, so these moves are described as general teacher choices rather than steps for specific year groups. Real connection still comes from the teacher knowing the students, while AI helps generate options. When schools configure tutor avatars, they can consider neutral avatars or no human face at all.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text states that research has not supported the idea that teaching to a student's preferred style improves learning (Pashler et al., 2008). It also reports that in two experiments, the race, gender, and age of an AI tutor's avatar shaped how much learners trusted it and whether they used its guidance (Anthis & Kyriakidou-Zacharoudiou, 2026). Some avatars were judged more credible than others for reasons unrelated to the quality of the help. The text does not provide a separate evidence label or additional figures beyond these findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text warns that AI can fall back on stereotypes, so the teacher must check that examples are accurate and respectful. It also makes clear that real connection comes from the teacher knowing the students, not from AI alone. Schools configuring tutors should consider neutral avatars, or no human face at all, to avoid building avatar biases into learning. The decisions about which formats to offer, which examples to use, and how avatars are set up stay with people. The text does not claim that format variety should be used to match a supposed learning style.
